GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE
EDUCATIONAL CONTENT LIBRARY
CHAPTER 02
Types and Forms of
Gender-Based Violence
A detailed, survivor-centred educational chapter with definitions, warning signs, practical scenarios, learning
activities, and sources.
EDUCATIONAL DRAFT - NOT YET APPROVED FOR PUBLICATION. Specialist safeguarding, legal, clinical,
translation and Rwanda referral verification are required. This chapter is not a diagnostic tool, legal opinion,
emergency service, or substitute for professional assistance.

Chapter learning objectives
After working through this chapter, a reader should be able to identify several forms of gender-based violence
(GBV), explain why harmful acts can overlap, recognize patterns of control without diagnosing a situation from a
checklist, understand barriers to disclosure, and identify safer routes to information, health care and specialist
support.
A note to readers: This chapter discusses violence, including non-graphic references to sexual abuse and
threats. You may skip any section. You are not required to remember or disclose personal experiences,
complete activities, confront anyone, or prove that harm has occurred. Read only when and where it feels safe.
1. Understanding what counts as GBV
Gender-based violence refers to harmful actions directed against people because of gender or unequal
gender-related power relations. It can occur in private and public, in person and through technology. It includes
physical, sexual, psychological and economic harm, threats, coercion, and deprivation of liberty. Women and
girls experience GBV disproportionately, while people of any gender may be affected. [1-3]
The word form describes how abuse is carried out - for example, a threat, an unwanted sexual act, or
withholding money as a means of control. The word setting describes where or in which relationship it occurs -
for example, within a partnership, at school, in a workplace, or online. A single incident can involve multiple
forms in more than one setting.
Not every disagreement or financial difficulty is violence. To understand a concerning situation, consider
whether there is coercion, intimidation, non-consent, a pattern of domination, threats or intentional harm, and
the wider context. A survivor should not be expected to collect evidence or label their experience before they
deserve respectful support.
2. Physical violence
Physical violence includes using physical force to injure, hurt, frighten, restrain, or control another person. It
may include pushing, hitting, kicking, burning, restraining someone against their will, or preventing access to
necessary medical care. Physical violence is serious even when it leaves no visible mark. [2,4]
Common warning signs and misunderstandings
(cid:127) A person describes being grabbed, restrained, threatened with a weapon, or physically punished for
disobedience.
(cid:127) Someone is prevented from leaving a place, obtaining urgent care, or seeking help after an injury.
(cid:127) A partner or family member minimizes an assault as “discipline,” “love,” or a one-time mistake.
Visible injuries are not required for someone to experience harm. Conversely, an injury alone does not establish
who caused it; professional assessment should be sensitive to context and safety. Assault involving
strangulation or pressure to the neck may cause serious injury even without obvious marks and needs urgent
medical assessment.
Case A - An argument at home
Scenario: During a disagreement, a partner pushes another person against a wall, blocks the door and warns
them not to speak to relatives.

How to understand it: The pushing and restriction of movement are physical acts; the warning and isolation
are also psychological or controlling behaviors.
Safer response: A supporter should first consider immediate safety, avoid confronting the person using
violence, and offer access to trusted professional support.
3. Sexual violence and sexual coercion
Sexual violence involves sexual acts, attempted acts or unwanted sexual contact or attention imposed without
free agreement, including by force, threats, manipulation, or misuse of authority. It may be committed by a
stranger, acquaintance, spouse, partner, teacher, supervisor or other person. Being in a marriage or
relationship does not create permanent consent. [1,3,7]
Consent must be freely given, informed, specific and revocable. Silence, fear, freezing, previous agreement,
intoxication, or dependence on another person do not establish freely given consent. The legal treatment of
specific acts and ages varies by jurisdiction; trained local practitioners must interpret relevant laws.
Sexual harassment, exploitation, and abuse
Sexual harassment can involve unwelcome sexual comments, pressure, messages, advances or touching.
Sexual exploitation involves abusing a position of vulnerability, trust or authority for sexual purposes. Examples
include demanding sexual favors in exchange for a job opportunity or essential assistance. Children need
child-protection responses, and adults should never ask children to describe abuse in detail outside a trained
safeguarding process.
Case B - A job opportunity
Scenario: A supervisor implies that a trainee will lose a placement unless they agree to unwanted sexual
contact.
How to understand it: This involves pressure backed by an unequal power relationship, potentially sexual
harassment, coercion and exploitation.
Safer response: The trainee should not be required to confront the supervisor or file a complaint before being
offered confidential information on independent reporting and support options.
Time-sensitive health consideration: Following sexual assault, seek medical attention as soon as safely
possible. Clinicians can assess injuries, sexually transmitted infection risks, pregnancy prevention and other
needs. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), when indicated, should start as soon as possible and no later
than 72 hours after possible exposure; other care remains valuable even after that window. [7,8]
4. Psychological and emotional violence
Psychological abuse involves actions that intimidate, degrade, manipulate, isolate, threaten or undermine a
person. Emotional abuse is commonly used to describe repeated humiliation, belittling, threats, guilt-based
control, or attacks on self-worth. These terms overlap; one incident or pattern may cause harm even without
physical violence. [2,3,4]
Examples include threats of harm, repeated insults, forcing isolation from family, using children to threaten a
caregiver, or deliberately creating fear. “Gaslighting” is a non-clinical popular term often used for attempts to
cause someone to doubt their perceptions; it should not replace clear descriptions of actual conduct.

It is important not to diagnose an entire relationship from a single insensitive comment. Look instead at
coercion, power, repeated behavior, the ability to disagree safely, and impact on autonomy. No one needs a
formal label to ask for support.
Case C - Messages and isolation
Scenario: A student is told by their partner that all friendships are disloyal. The partner repeatedly insults the
student, monitors every conversation, and threatens to spread rumors.
How to understand it: Repeated intimidation, humiliation and forced isolation may amount to psychological
abuse and coercive control.
Safer response: Avoid urging a public confrontation. Ask whether it is safe to communicate, whether devices
are monitored, and what support the student would prefer.
5. Economic and financial abuse
Economic abuse uses money, access to work, education, property or essential resources to limit a person’s
independence or control their decisions. It can include confiscating earnings, denying access to basic
necessities as punishment, sabotaging employment, coercing debt, or preventing someone from attending
school. [2,3]
Economic abuse is not identical to poverty or a jointly agreed household budget. The distinguishing concern is
coercive restriction, exploitation or deprivation rather than limited income alone. A person may be unable to
leave an unsafe relationship because of dependent children, lack of transport, housing insecurity or fear of
losing school fees.
Case D - A family business
Scenario: A married person works daily in a family shop, but their partner confiscates all earnings, forbids paid
employment elsewhere and withholds transport money as punishment for visiting friends.
How to understand it: This may involve economic control combined with isolation.
Safer response: A supporter can discuss safe and discreet access to services, documents, income-related
advice and practical help without insisting that the person leave immediately.
6. Technology-facilitated GBV
Technology-facilitated abuse uses phones, social media, messaging platforms, location-sharing services or
other digital tools to threaten, track, shame, exploit or control a person. Offline and online forms often overlap.
Some acts include repeated threatening messages, unauthorized access to accounts, tracking location without
consent, publication of private information, and sharing intimate images without permission. [2,5]
A person experiencing technology-facilitated abuse may fear that changing passwords, deleting an app or
blocking someone could escalate danger. Safety decisions should consider whether the other person has
device access or controls accounts. Digital safety guidance should be personalized by a trained practitioner
when risk is high.
Case E - Online threats
Scenario: A former partner threatens to publish private photographs unless a person resumes contact and
shares their current location.

How to understand it: Threats, image-based abuse and coercive control may be present even when no
physical contact occurs.
Safer response: Do not forward images or encourage public retaliation. Seek safe specialist support, consider
reporting platform abuse when appropriate, and preserve information only if it is safe and lawful to do so.
7. Social, reproductive and identity-related coercion
Some violence occurs through controlling social participation, mobility, marriage choices or reproductive
decisions. Examples include forced marriage, threats for refusing a relationship, interference with access to
reproductive healthcare, or restricting movement for gender-based reasons. Forms of reproductive coercion
may include pressure concerning pregnancy or contraception. [3,9]
People may also be targeted because they do not conform to gender expectations. Faith, family and cultural
background can be important sources of resilience, but no cultural or religious justification excuses violence or
forced participation. Local law, child protection rules and clinical practice must be checked before providing
legal or medical instructions.

9. How forms of GBV overlap
Forms of violence should not be treated as separate boxes. One individual may experience control of their
finances, humiliation, threats of sexual harm and digital monitoring simultaneously. Understanding these
connections helps avoid the mistaken belief that only physical injury makes an experience serious. The
European Institute for Gender Equality describes a continuum of violence in which forms can reinforce one
another. [6]
For example, a controlling partner may make a person financially dependent, demand constant location sharing,
threaten family members and then use physical force when challenged. The overlapping pattern can create

10. Recognizing risk without creating a checklist diagnosis
Warning signs include threats, escalating intimidation, forced isolation, monitoring, stalking, coercive sexual
demands, unwanted physical restraint, and deliberate restriction of necessities. These signs help people notice
possible danger but cannot predict an individual’s future actions reliably. Safety is a practical priority even when
a situation does not fit a textbook pattern.
If someone is in immediate danger, the safest response may be to move toward a safer place and contact
available emergency or specialist services, if doing so will not increase risk. Avoid telling a person to challenge
an abuser, secretly record conversations or leave in a particular way; those decisions require context-sensitive
planning.
11. Effects on survivors and why reactions differ
Possible consequences include injuries, fear, shame, distress, traumatic stress reactions, difficulty
concentrating, disrupted education or work, reduced trust, financial loss and social isolation. Responses vary:
some people disclose promptly, some remain silent, and others may show no obvious emotional reaction. None
of these responses establishes whether harm occurred. [1,7]
A person may remain in contact with someone who has harmed them because of threats, affection, children,
finances, disability-related needs, lack of trusted services or other circumstances. Support should focus on
informed choices and safety, not judging the survivor’s behavior.
12. Survivor-centred first-line support
WHO describes a structured approach known as LIVES: Listen, Inquire about needs and concerns, Validate,
Enhance safety, and Support. This is a framework for trained providers; everyday supporters can adopt its
respectful principles without undertaking an investigation or counselling role. [10]
Principle What supportive behavior can sound like
Listen "You can share only what you want to share."
Inquire "What would be most useful or safest for you right now?"
Validate "What happened is not something you deserved."
Enhance safety "Would it help to discuss a safe person or place with a trained worker?"
Support "I can help you find available services if you want."
Do not demand a detailed story, promise total secrecy, blame the survivor, press for forgiveness or
reconciliation, or contact a suspected perpetrator without a safe and lawful basis. Professionals must explain
confidentiality limits and child safeguarding or reporting obligations applicable to their work.

lines.text: 13. Helping children and adolescents safely
When a child may be experiencing violence, protection takes priority over adult learning activities. Do not
interview repeatedly, ask leading questions, request images, or promise to keep everything secret. Listen
calmly, explain what help may be needed in age-appropriate words, and contact a qualified child protection or
health professional through established procedures. Children cannot be expected to manage adult safety plans
independently.
In Rwanda, the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion publishes the National Child Development Agency
hotline 711. Availability and appropriate referral procedures should be verified at the time of use. [11]
14. Safe information seeking in Rwanda
Rwanda’s Isange One Stop Centres provide coordinated services that may include medical assistance,
psychosocial support and justice-related services. UNHCR Rwanda lists a toll-free contact number of 3029 and
notes that approaching a centre may result in a GBV incident being reported to law enforcement. A person
should ask about confidentiality and reporting implications when it is safe to do so. [11,12]

15. Practical learning activities
Activity 1 - Identify the form, not the person
Read each fictional example and name possible forms of harm: (a) A partner takes wages and prevents school
attendance. (b) A supervisor demands sexual contact in exchange for a promotion. (c) An ex-partner repeatedly
threatens to publish private images. (d) A relative restrains someone during a dispute. More than one form may
apply.
Activity 2 - Separate conflict from coercive control
Compare two situations. In the first, two partners respectfully disagree over shared expenses and agree to
revisit the budget. In the second, one partner keeps all money, threatens punishment for disagreement and
blocks employment. Ask: What makes the second situation more concerning? Look for coercion, threats, power
and loss of choice, not just the presence of disagreement.

lines.text: Activity 3 - Choose supportive language
Consider which response protects dignity: "Why did you not leave earlier?" or "What support would feel safe
and helpful to you?" Explain why the second is more appropriate. Do not use this exercise to pressure anyone
to describe their own experience.
Activity 4 - Map safe support options
Without entering names, addresses or personal details, identify general types of support that may exist: a
trusted adult, health centre, trained GBV worker, child protection worker, legal information provider or
emergency service. Think about which route would be accessible, private and safe in a hypothetical situation.
Activity 5 - Responsible online response
A friend says their images are being threatened online. What should you avoid doing? Consider why forwarding
the image, public confrontation, posting screenshots or using their account without permission may create more
harm. Identify a safer first response, such as listening and offering information about trained support.
16. Knowledge assessment
1. Can GBV happen without physical injuries?
Yes. Sexual, psychological, economic and digital forms can occur without visible injuries.
2. Does marriage mean a person has permanently consented to sex?
No. Consent must be freely given and remains specific and revocable.
3. Is every financial disagreement economic abuse?
No. Coercive control, deprivation, threats and context distinguish abuse from ordinary disagreement.
4. Can one incident involve multiple forms?
Yes. A physical assault may also involve threats, sexual coercion or economic control.
5. Should a supporter ask for a detailed account to verify what happened?
No. Do not investigate or demand repeated disclosure. Offer respectful support and professional referral.
6. Is digital surveillance harmless when no physical contact occurs?
No. Technology can be used to intimidate, monitor or control someone.
7. What is an important time window after possible HIV exposure?
PEP assessment is time-sensitive; when indicated, it should begin as soon as possible and within 72 hours.
8. Are response services automatically confidential in every circumstance?
No. Explain that legal, safeguarding or reporting requirements may limit confidentiality.
9. Who can experience GBV?
People of any gender, while women and girls are disproportionately affected.
10. What is the first priority when someone is in immediate danger?
Consider immediate safety and appropriate urgent support; avoid actions that could escalate danger.

17. Facilitator guidance and safeguarding
A facilitator should inform learners about potentially distressing content before a session. Participation in
scenarios and reflections must be optional. Never ask for personal testimonies or facilitate public identification
of survivors. Provide private, verified information about support channels; explain the limits of privacy and
mandatory reporting. Train facilitators to respond calmly to unexpected disclosures and to refer rather than
investigate.
For publication on VUGA NDAKUMVA, every example and self-help activity should be reviewed for child
safeguarding, disability access, plain-language comprehension, realistic Rwanda context and safe use on
potentially monitored devices. Avoid analytics or notification designs that could inadvertently reveal a user’s
interest in GBV content.
18. Key messages and glossary
Key messages. GBV has many interrelated forms. Visible injury is not required for harm to be serious. Consent
and personal autonomy matter. A survivor deserves non-judgmental support whether or not they report an
incident. Safe professional assistance can include health, protection, psychosocial and justice services,
depending on needs and wishes.
Term Plain-language explanation
Coercion Pressure or threats used to make someone do something against their free choice
Consent A freely given, specific and changeable agreement
Survivor-centred An approach prioritizing dignity, safety, informed choice and respectful support
Economic abuse Use of financial or material control to cause harm or reduce independence
Digital abuse Harm or coercion carried out or amplified through technology
Intimate partner violence Abusive behavior by a current or former partner
Safeguarding Steps to prevent and respond to harm, particularly involving children or vulnerable
people
